name: Darnel
what: Lolium temulentum, a ryegrass. Until it heads, it is all but indistinguishable from wheat — same height, same colour, same leaf. Its seed is commonly infected with a fungus that causes dizziness and nausea; the Latin temulentum means drunken.
why: The parable's central instruction — let both grow together until the harvest — is not patience as a virtue. It is agronomy. You cannot pull darnel early because you cannot identify it early, and by the time you can, the roots are tangled with the wheat. Knowing the weed turns a moral into a practical observation.

name: Mustard
what: Brassica nigra. The seed is about 1 mm across; the plant reaches 2–3 m in a single season. Not a tree — a fast, rangy annual herb.
why: Two things English loses. “The smallest of all seeds” is not literally true and a farmer knew it — it is the smallest seed anyone routinely sowed. And mustard is a weed: it self-seeds aggressively and Jewish agricultural custom kept it out of tidy garden beds. A man deliberately sowing it in his field is a slightly subversive image, not a charming one.

name: Fig
what: Ficus carica. The early fruit — paggim — swells at the same time as or slightly before the leaves open. Leaves are therefore a promise of fruit.
why: A fig in full leaf with nothing on it is genuinely anomalous, which is why the cursing lands for a first-century listener. Mark alone adds “for it was not the season for figs” — the clause that makes the act arbitrary, and so marks it as a sign rather than a grievance. Matthew removes it.

name: Mulberry & sycamore-fig
what: Two unrelated trees. The sykaminos is Morus nigra, the black mulberry — deep, stubborn roots. The sykomorea is Ficus sycomorus, a broad fig with low limbs that a short man can scramble into.
why: Luke uses both, four chapters apart, and English blurs them. At 17:6 faith uproots the deep-rooted mulberry — the point is the roots. At 19:4 Zacchaeus climbs the low-branched sycamore-fig — the point is that it is climbable. Same English word, opposite properties.

name: Mint, dill, cumin, rue
what: Kitchen-garden herbs of negligible value. The Torah commands tithing grain, wine and oil; tithing herbs is scrupulous extension, not obligation.
why: The lists do not match. Matthew 23:23 has mint, dill and cumin. Luke 11:42 has mint, rue and “every herb”. Rue was not even subject to tithe under later rabbinic ruling — so Luke's version sharpens the absurdity. A diff you can see only at the level of the individual plant.

name: “Lilies” of the field
what: Almost certainly not a lily. The likeliest candidates are the scarlet Anemone coronaria or the crown daisy — common Galilean wildflowers that blanket the hills in spring and are gone in weeks.
why: The saying compares them to Solomon in all his glory. A cultivated white lily is a luxury flower; a wild anemone is a weed nobody planted, nobody tends, and that dies within the month. The comparison is far sharper if the flower is worthless.

name: Olive
what: Olea europaea. Gethsemane is Aramaic gat shemanim — oil press. The Mount of Olives was terraced groves with presses cut into the rock.
why: The garden is named for a machine that crushes olives to extract oil. Luke alone records the sweat like drops of blood, in a place whose name means press. Neither writer comments on it; the geography does the work.

name: Hyssop
what: Origanum syriacum, Syrian marjoram. A small, sprawling herb with short woody stems — nothing like a pole.
why: At the crucifixion a sponge is raised to Jesus' mouth on hyssop (John 19:29). The stems are too short to reach a crucified man, which has made some suggest the text originally read hyssō — “on a javelin”. John alone uses the plant, and hyssop is the herb that daubed the doorposts at Passover. The awkward botany may be the point.

name: Barley
what: The cheap grain — coarse, fast-growing, harvested before wheat, and eaten by the poor and by animals. It cost roughly a third the price of wheat.
why: Only John specifies that the five loaves are barley. The other three leave the grain unnamed. It is a single adjective, and it quietly makes the boy's lunch the food of the poorest person present.

name: Thorns
what: A catch-all for the region's spiny scrub — Sarcopoterium, Ziziphus, centaury. Fast, opportunistic, and the first thing to reclaim untended ground.
why: In the sower, thorns do not attack the seed; they simply grow faster and take the light. The parable names the mechanism: nothing is destroyed, it is crowded out — which is what the interpretation then says about wealth and worry.

name: Dog & little dog
what: Two different words. Kyōn is the street dog — scavenger, unclean, an insult. Kynarion is its diminutive: the small dog that lives in the house and is fed there.
why: To the Syrophoenician woman, Jesus does not use the insult. He uses the diminutive, and she answers inside the same image — even the little dogs under the table eat the children's crumbs. English prints “dogs” for both and turns a domestic metaphor into a slur.

name: Sparrow
what: The cheapest meat sold — trapped, skewered and sold to the poor. An assarion is one-sixteenth of a day's wage.
why: Matthew 10:29: two sparrows for an assarion. Luke 12:6: five for two assaria. Buy in bulk and the fifth bird is free — and that is the bird the saying is about, the one thrown in for nothing, not forgotten before God. The bulk discount is the argument, and only the diff shows it.

name: Camel & needle
what: The largest animal in regular use and the smallest everyday aperture. The much-repeated “Needle Gate” in Jerusalem — a low postern a camel could squeeze through on its knees — has no ancient evidence whatsoever; it appears first in medieval commentary.
why: The image is meant to be impossible, not merely difficult. Softening it into a gate makes the disciples' reaction — then who can be saved? — incomprehensible. The honest reading is the absurd one.

name: Fox
what: In Greek fable the fox is cunning. In rabbinic idiom it is the small animal — the saying “be a tail to lions rather than a head to foxes” sets it against the lion as the inferior.
why: When Jesus calls Herod “that fox”, the Greek reading makes it sly and the Jewish reading makes it petty — a pretender, not a lion. The second is almost certainly the insult intended, and it is invisible in English.

name: Swine
what: Unclean, and therefore not raised by Jews — a herd of two thousand marks the territory as gentile. Pigs cannot swim well and panic in water.
why: The herd locates the exorcism on the far, gentile shore. It also collides with the geography: Matthew names the Gergesenes, Mark and Luke the Gadarenes, and Gadara sits 10 km inland with no steep bank for a herd to run down. The animals are evidence in a textual dispute.

name: Hen & chicks
what: A farmyard bird gathering chicks under her wings — the one image in the gospels where Jesus compares himself to a female animal.
why: It arrives at the climax of the lament over Jerusalem, immediately before the temple is called desolate. A hen covering chicks is a posture of protection that offers the mother's own body as the shelter, and it is the last thing said before the city's house is left empty.

name: Talent
what: A weight of silver, roughly 6,000 denarii — about twenty years of a labourer's wages for a single talent.
why: The unforgiving servant owes ten thousand talents: sixty million denarii, on the order of 160,000 years of daily wages. It is not a large debt, it is an unpayable one, deliberately absurd. His fellow servant owes a hundred denarii — about three months. The ratio is 600,000 to one, and that ratio is the parable.

name: Lepton & quadrans
what: The lepton is the smallest coin in circulation — two of them make one Roman quadrans, which is one sixty-fourth of a day's wage.
why: Mark writes “two lepta, which make a quadrans” — stopping to convert a Greek coin into Roman money. He does this repeatedly, and it is one of the clearest internal signals that Mark is writing for a Roman audience. Luke, telling the same story, does not bother.

name: Denarius
what: Explicitly the daily rate for a field labourer (Matthew 20:2). The standard unit against which every other sum in the gospels can be read.
why: It makes the other numbers legible. The nard poured out at Bethany is valued at 300 denarii — most of a year's income, destroyed in a gesture. The two denarii left with the innkeeper for the beaten man is two days' care, quietly generous. Neither registers without the rate.

name: Stater
what: A silver tetradrachm — four drachmas, equal to two didrachma, and the temple tax was one didrachmon per man.
why: The coin in the fish's mouth is the exact amount for two people, Peter and Jesus, and not a drachma more. The miracle is denominated precisely; Matthew, the tax collector's gospel, is the only one that records it.

name: Seah & cor
what: A saton is roughly 13 litres of flour; a koros is about 230 litres — a large agricultural unit.
why: “Three measures of meal” in the leaven parable is about 40 litres of flour — enough bread for a hundred people, hidden by one woman. The quantity is extravagant and almost always read past. In the dishonest manager, the debts written down are hundreds of litres of oil and wheat: the fraud is industrial in scale.

name: Three nets
what: An amphiblēstron is a circular cast net, thrown by one man from the shore. A sagēnē is a dragnet — a long seine worked between boats that sweeps everything in its path. Diktyon is the generic word.
why: Simon and Andrew are casting the one-man net when they are called. The kingdom parable of the net uses the dragnet — the one that takes everything indiscriminately and sorts afterwards, which is precisely the parable's point. English flattens all three into “net” and the distinction dies.

name: Two baskets
what: A kophinos is the small stiff provision basket a Jewish traveller carried — Roman satirists mocked Jews for it. A spyris is a large hamper; it is the basket Paul is lowered over the Damascus wall in, big enough to hold a man.
why: Across all four gospels kophinos appears 6 times and spyris 4 — and they never cross. Every small basket belongs to the feeding of the five thousand, every large one to the four thousand. Twelve for the tribes, seven for the nations. Wholly invisible in English.

name: Wineskin
what: A whole goat hide, sewn and sealed. New wine ferments and releases gas; a fresh skin stretches to take the pressure. A skin that has already stretched once is brittle and has no give left.
why: The saying is not about novelty versus tradition in the abstract. It is a material fact: the old skin does not resist the new wine out of stubbornness — it physically cannot flex again, and it bursts, losing both. Luke adds a line the others omit: nobody who has drunk old wine wants new, for he says the old is better.

name: Unshrunk cloth
what: Unfulled wool shrinks hard the first time it is washed. Patching old cloth with it guarantees the patch will contract and tear away, taking the surrounding fabric with it.
why: Paired with the wineskin, and doing the same work from the opposite direction: the new does not fail to fit the old out of incompatibility of spirit, but because of what the materials do. Both sayings are craft observations before they are anything else.

name: Millstone
what: Two kinds. The hand mill a woman turns is a stone you can lift. The mylos onikos — the “donkey millstone” — is the great upper stone of a village mill, turned by an animal and weighing hundreds of kilos.
why: The saying specifies the donkey stone. It is not a millstone but the largest one in the village — an object no person could lift, let alone remove once sunk. The adjective carries the whole weight of the threat.

name: Lamp, basket, stand
what: A lychnos is a small clay oil lamp with a floating wick. A modios is a dry measure of about 9 litres — an opaque wooden or pottery vessel.
why: Putting a lamp under a modios does not dim it. It smothers it: the vessel cuts off air and the flame gutters out within moments. The saying is usually read as concealment. Its mechanism is suffocation.

name: Winnowing fork & threshing floor
what: A flat wooden shovel, and a hard swept circle of rock, usually sited on a ridge to catch the evening wind. Threshed grain is tossed up; the breeze carries the light chaff aside and the heavy kernels fall back.
why: John the Baptist's image is a specific piece of equipment at a specific moment. The separation is not a judgement handed down from outside — it is the weight of the thing itself deciding where it lands in the wind.
